title: HR Process Automation: 13 HR Processes That Can Be Automated (And How to Do It)
summary: HR automation has AI that automates routine HR decisions — including timecard, time-off request and expense approvals — based on rules you set. See all 14 processes and what it takes to automate them.
body_markdown:
Automated decisioning logic is what separates Paycom’s automation from the HR software you already have. Other HR tools help you get to a task in your queue faster. Automated decisioning removes the task from your queue altogether.


Here are the HR decisions Paycom already makes without a person today:


- **time and attendance:** punch changes and timecards approved or denied against the criteria you preset
- **time off:** time-off requests decided in real time against staffing, consecutive days, hours worked, seniority and other criteria established by your organization
- **expenses:** reimbursements auto-approved against your spending policy, then fed to payroll
- **payroll:** pay errors caught throughout the pay period and routed to the employee with guidance to fix or resolve before submission


Paycom collectively calls the AI across its software “smart AI,” and it arrives already enabled, at no extra cost for usage. Your Paycom specialist configures it with you during implementation, so you won’t be building it on your own.


## What is HR automation?


HR automation completes routine HR tasks or processes, decreasing manual effort. Automated decisioning logic applies rules your organization configures to execute decisions and complete routine HR work across the employee life cycle. That covers approvals, denials, routing, task assignment and error-catching, all resolved before the request ever reaches a person.


The definition of HR automation stopped at speed. You automate the repetitive, time-consuming tasks so your HR team gets time back, and that still holds true. What has changed is that software can now return an actual decision rather than simply handing off the work more quickly. Automating punch change requests used to mean a manager got to it sooner. Today, the software approves them instantly based on the rule you wrote, reducing payroll processing and reporting delays.


You’ll see “HR automation,” “HR process automation” and “HR workflow automation” used interchangeably, and this article treats them as one topic. If you want the distinction, HR process automation describes automating an end-to-end process, such as onboarding. HR workflow automation refers to automating the routing and sequencing within that process. HR automation is the umbrella term covering both, plus the decisions made along the way.


Where the decision gets made is what separates “full-solution automation” from traditional automation. When your decisioning sits outside your system of record, every approval becomes a round trip between platforms, and every handoff gives stale data or data reentry a chance to produce the wrong call and expose the organization to risk. When the data sits inside a single database, automated decisioning logic reads live data and writes back to the same record. Paycom’s smart AI is[built within its proprietary single software](https://www.paycom.com/ai-standards/) , aiding users by eliminating decisions, steps and tasks across the HR life cycle.


It’s worth knowing what those routine manual decisions cost you. Each manual time-off review or approval can cost a company an average of $12.15 in labor, according to an[October 2025 EY study](https://www.paycom.com/resources/blog/cost-of-manual-hr-processes/) commissioned by Paycom. Multiply that by your head count, and the approval queue becomes a line item nobody budgets for.

Today, 14 HR processes are automation-ready: payroll, onboarding and offboarding, timekeeping, position management, performance management, time-off requests, expense management, tax forms, recruiting, background checks, compliance management, employee engagement, training and development, and benefits administration.

Here are some examples of where automated decisioning holds up in practice:


- a multisite hourly operation, such as a hotel group running 72 properties, where one manager approves dozens of identical punch corrections that meet the same rule every time
- a double-shift day, where two different pay rates must apply without a manual adjustment
- a late-week missed punch that would otherwise land after payroll closes and become a correction instead of a timecard edit
- a peak-season time-off blackout that applies across every location without a manager policing it
- a resignation already on file, where a last-minute time-off request should be caught and denied
- an employee on a performance improvement plan, where their time-off request should be routed for review rather than auto-decided


## How to automate HR processes


To automate HR processes, identify repetitive, rules-based work, set the criteria and exception paths, and configure the software to complete or route each task.


### *What automating a decision actually takes*


It’s worth pointing out that the setup is simpler than it sounds because many assume it will be a major IT project, which stops HR teams before they start.


In[Forrester’s Total Economic Impact™ study](https://tei.forrester.com/go/paycom/gone/) of Paycom’s Time-Off Requests featuring GONE, the HR director at a composite organization only spent 10 hours per month overseeing the implementation of the tool, roughly two hours to author or amend each decision rule, and one hour of self-paced training per manager. Against that setup, the organization experienced a projected three-year return on investment between 102% and 821%; up to 192 hours a year returned to HR, finance and administrative staff; up to 30 hours a year returned to each manager; and up to 240 overtime hours avoided annually from more consistent staffing.*


Payroll shows the same shape on a larger scale. A separate[commissioned TEI study conducted by Forrester Consulting for Paycom](https://www.paycom.com/resources/blog/forrester-tei-paycom-beti-cut-payroll-processing-time/) found that a 2,500-employee composite organization reduced the labor needed to process payroll by 90%, cut time spent correcting payroll errors by 85% and saved 2,600 hours annually.**


[Shamin Hotels](https://www.paycom.com/learn-more/hospitality-case-study/) , Virginia’s largest hotel operator, runs roughly 72 properties under Marriott, Hyatt, IHG and Hilton brands with over 3,000 associates. After consolidating onto a single database, the company reduced payroll processing time by 85%, and its administrators now save 20 hours a month through automated reporting because there are no APIs or integrations left to reconcile. Job changes, promotions and transfers that used to take weeks are now resolved in a matter of hours, and the executive team can save three hours a day by not having to navigate for data when using IWant.


### *Three rules of thumb for choosing what to automate first*


Use these three guidelines to prioritize the work that can deliver the most value with the least need for human judgment.


1. **Start where volume is highest and judgment is lowest.** Punch changes and policy-compliant expenses clear both tests immediately.
2. **Plan the exception path before activating the preferred path.** A rule you can’t work around gets switched off the first time it produces an adverse result.
3. **Automate the decision, not the notification.** If the output is an alert telling a manager to go decide something, the automation moves your queue rather than shrinking it.


What breaks when you skip this can become dramatic. A missed punch is a small problem that gets expensive with a delay. The employee must report it, and a manager must approve the fix. If either step happens after the pay period closes, it becomes a payroll correction with added wage-and-hour risk. Similarly, a final paycheck missed on a state deadline is a penalty rather than a rework item. An expense approved without being read is an audit finding waiting for a sample. These problems don’t announce themselves. They accumulate quietly and land on your HR team.


At the multistate and multicountry scale, that lag compounds. A rule you set once and apply identically is also the only version of a policy you can produce on demand during an audit, and that becomes more important as your number of jurisdictions, sites, pay structures and union agreements grows. Paycom’s automated payroll experience, Beti, is available to companies organized in the U.S., Mexico, Canada, the United Kingdom and Ireland, and[Global HCM™](https://global.paycom.com/) can operate across sites and locations in more than 190 countries.


That leaves one more question: Do you have to build any of this yourself? With Paycom, you don’t. The smart AI is enabled and configured through implementation, and you set your decision rules during a guided setup with your Paycom specialist.


## How do HR automation tools optimize workflow?


### *Automated vs. assisted: What the tool hands back*


ADP, Workday, UKG, Paylocity and Rippling all market AI capability in HR, as do workflow automation platforms and IT service vendors. Tools cover two very different things, and that distinction is the one worth questioning.


**Dimension** **Assisted** **Automated**


What it returns Information, a draft or a signal An approval, denial or routed outcome


Who decides A person, after reading it The rule you configured


Effect on the queue Same length, reached faster Shorter


Where it runs Often a layer above the record Inside the system of record


What it needs from you Someone available to act Criteria set once


How you audit it The person’s judgment The rule, the data it read, the timestamp


What it costs when it’s wrong A bad call, traceable to a person A bad rule you fix once, for every future request


Both assisted and automated tools are marketed as HR automation. When you compare tools, the question worth asking is whether the software actually reduces decisions, rather than whether it uses AI. Ask each vendor whether its software makes decisions without a person involved and to show you how it does so. If a description stops at surfacing insights, what you’re looking at is traditional HR automation, and nothing is reducing the routine decisions in your workforce.


## Is automated HR decision-making compliant?


It depends on governance, and in at least one state, the bar is now statutory. Colorado’s SB24-205 never took effect after a federal court paused it in April 2026. Colorado replaced it with[SB26-189](https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb26-189) , signed May 14, 2026, and effective Jan. 1, 2027. The new law still covers notice when automated decision-making technology is used in consequential decisions, correction of factually incorrect personal data and meaningful human review after an adverse outcome. Employment decisions sit squarely in scope.


Four properties separate decisioning you can defend from decisioning you’ll switch off in a month:


- **The decisions are named.** You can list them: punch changes, timecards, PTO, expenses, reimbursements and knockout responses.
- **The rules are yours and editable.** You set configurable criteria during a guided setup, and you can change them without a support ticket and produce them on demand.
- **The decision reads live data from one place.** A single-database architecture means the rule reads the same record it writes to, and your data isn’t shared across multiple third parties.
- **Someone is accountable when it’s wrong.** Paycom’s AI developments and enhancements are overseen, tested and reviewed prior to deployment, then monitored and reevaluated in use by multiple departments and a data protection officer, with AI governance routinely reported to the Board of Directors. That is backed by[five ISO certifications](https://www.paycom.com/ai-standards/) , including ISO/IEC 42001, the world’s first AI management system standard.


Human oversight works as a design principle here rather than a footnote. While AI can often be the smartest tech in the stack, it lacks the strength of human instinct, so that oversight remains vital for secure, compliant and accountable operations. It includes a service model built on a single point of human contact, which AI can enhance but never replace.


## Will automated decisioning logic replace HR jobs?


No. Automated decisioning absorbs the rules-based layer of the work, including approvals, denials, routing, task assignment and error detection. Judgment remains with your people, including investigations, restructuring, employee relations, culture, negotiation and the final call on anything consequential.


The realistic read is that the roles stay and the job description changes. You’ll spend more of your time designing the policy that the automated decisioning logic enforces and owning the exceptions it routes to you. The human side of the work hasn’t gotten any easier either.[SHRM’s 2026 Talent Trends](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/research/2026-talent-trends) found that more than two-thirds of HR professionals are still struggling to fill roles. Automated decisioning won’t solve that for you, but it can stop the approval queue from eating the hours you need to work on it.

## Frequently asked questions about HR automation


### ***What is HR process automation?***


HR process automation involves automating an end-to-end HR process, such as onboarding or payroll, rather than a single step inside it. In everyday use, it means the same thing as HR automation.


### ***What is HR workflow automation?***


HR workflow automation is automating the routing and sequencing within a process: who receives a task, in what order, and what happens when it’s complete. Automated HR workflows can also decide the outcome, not just move the request along.


### ***Can HR decisions be automated?***


Yes, the rules-based parts of it. Approvals, denials, routing, task assignment and error-catching can all run on decisioning criteria you configure. Judgment calls, investigations and employee relations stay with your people.


### ***How do I set up automated decisioning logic?***


With Paycom, you don’t build it on your own. The smart AI arrives enabled and configured through implementation. You set the decision criteria during a guided setup with your Paycom specialist, and you can update them without a support ticket using easy guided setup tools.


### ***What HR decisions can be automated for small teams?***


The same ones, and the case is stronger because a small team feels every approval. Start with punch changes, timecards, time-off decisions and policy-compliant expense approvals.


### ***Is HR automation the same as AI in HR?***


No. HR automation is the broad use of software to complete HR work with less manual effort. AI is one way to power that automation, and automated decisioning logic is one type of AI that applies your configured rules to approve, deny or route routine HR and payroll requests.


### ***What is HRIS automation?***


HRIS automation is automation delivered inside your human resources information system, so employee data entered once populates systemwide instead of being rekeyed into payroll, time and benefits separately.


### ***What is HR automation software?***


HR automation software decides and completes routine HR work rather than routing it to a person. The test is whether the vendor can name the decisions its software makes without human involvement.


### ***How much does it cost to automate an HR decision?***


The cost depends on the provider. Some HR software vendors charge for AI usage through token credits, usage tiers or price increases that may not be clear upfront. Paycom owns its data centers and builds its software and AI tools in-house, so clients do not pay an additional fee to use Paycom’s AI tools.


### ***How does automation improve HR compliance workflows?***


It applies the same rule to every request and records what was decided, on what data, under which rule and when. That consistency is what survives an audit.


### ***Does automated HR decision-making comply with AI law?***


That comes down to governance. Look for configurable rules you can produce on demand, documented oversight, human review of exceptions, an audit trail and certifications such as ISO/IEC 42001.[Colorado’s SB26-189](https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb26-189) , signed May 14, 2026, and effective Jan. 1, 2027, includes requirements tied to notice, correction of factually incorrect personal data and meaningful human review after an adverse outcome.


### *Do we have to build or configure the AI ourselves?*


Not on your own. The smart AI arrives already enabled and configured through implementation, and decision rules are set with your Paycom specialist during a guided setup.


### ***Will automated decisioning logic replace HR?***


No. It takes over repetitive, rules-based tasks. Judgment stays with people, and emerging state law increasingly requires human review of adverse, AI-influenced employment decisions.
